title: Take Home Exercise 1
text:
This take-home exercise investigates the spatial (“where”) and spatio-temporal (“where + when”) patterns of new business registrations in Singapore between 1 Jan 2024 and 30 Jun 2025. Using the ACRA “Information on Corporate Entities” datasets and SSIC 2020 classifications, we select at least three business types (2- or 3-digit SSIC) and analyse how their locations and intensities evolve over time.
Our workflow mirrors the point-pattern framework taught in class:

Data wrangling & geocoding: tidy ACRA records, standardise dates/SSIC codes, and geocode by postal code via OneMap; convert to sf with SVY21 (EPSG:3414).
Exploratory mapping: counts by subzone/planning area to establish baseline patterns.
First-order analysis (intensity): Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) to reveal spatial hot spots for each SSIC and period.
Second-order analysis (dependence): Ripley’s K / CSR envelopes to test whether registrations are clustered, random, or dispersed.
Spatio-temporal analysis: STKDE (monthly slices) to detect emerging, persistent, and fading clusters over the study window.

The results are communicated through cartographic maps and concise figure captions words , followed by a synthesis translating findings into urban land-use and economic development implications**—e.g., infrastructure readiness, zoning flexibility, activation of under-served subzones, and monitoring of over-concentration risks.

text:
2 The Data
This study uses ACRA corporate entity registrations combined with reference layers and services to enable spatial and spatio-temporal analysis.

2.1 Data sources










Dataset Name
Description
Format
Provider
Notes




ACRA – Information on Corporate Entities (A–Z, Others)
All entity registrations. Used to extract new businesses by SSIC and date.
CSV (27 files)
data.gov.sg / ACRA
Split alphabetically: A–Z plus a 27th file for names starting with digits/symbols.


SSIC 2020
Singapore Standard Industrial Classification; used to choose business types (2-/3-/5-digit).
CSV/XLSX
SingStat
We derive ssic2, ssic3 and use primary_ssic_code.


OneMap Search API
Geocoding service to convert postal codes to coordinates.
Web API
SLA / OneMap
Returns WGS84 (lat/lon). We transform to SVY21 (EPSG:3414).


Master Plan Subzones (MPSZ 2024)
Administrative subzone polygons for aggregation and mapping.
GPKG/Shapefile
data.gov.sg / URA/SLA
Reprojected to SVY21 (EPSG:3414) for analysis.





2.2 Fields used (ACRA)








Field
Meaning
Example




uen
Unique Entity Number (entity identifier)
201912345K


entity_name
Registered business name
ABC PTE. LTD.


registration_incorporation_date
Registration date (YYYY-MM-DD)
2025-03-14


primary_ssic_code
Primary SSIC code (2/3/4/5-digit)
56111


postal_code
Registered postal code (should be 6 digits)
018989


entity_type / status
Type/status if required for filtering
LIVE COMPANY




Additional columns may exist in different ACRA dumps; we standardise names with janitor::clean_names() and coalesce equivalent fields where needed.



2.3 Study coverage

Temporal window: 1 Jan 2024 – 30 Jun 2025 (inclusive).

Spatial extent: Singapore national boundary; mapping/aggregation by subzone and planning area.

Business scope: At least three SSIC types (2- or 3-digit groups, or 5-digit subclasses), selected prior to analysis.



2.4 Pre-processing & wrangling (summary)

Read and row-bind all 27 ACRA CSVs; add source_file for provenance.

Standardise fields: parse registration_incorporation_date as Date (UTC), derive year, month.

Postal code hygiene: keep digits only, left-pad to 6; drop non-6-digit values before geocoding.

Deduplicate by uen + registration_incorporation_date (if necessary).

Filter to the target SSIC code set and to the study window.

Geocode unique postal codes via OneMap; join X/Y back to ACRA records.

Convert to sf (WGS84) → transform to SVY21 (EPSG:3414) for distance-based methods.

Join subzone attributes; save intermediates as RDS for reproducibility.



2.5 Data quality & limitations

Geocoding precision: Postal codes resolve to building/entrance centroids, not unit-level; some industrial sites share codes.

Registration vs. operation: Registration date ≠ opening date; counts reflect legal registrations.

Address anomalies: Legacy/PO box or malformed postcodes may not geocode; these are excluded.

Classification drift: SSIC codes can change over time; we use the recorded primary_ssic_code as-is.



2.6 Coordinate reference systems (CRS)

Input: WGS84 (EPSG:4326) from OneMap.

Analysis/Maps: SVY21 / Singapore TM (EPSG:3414), metres, suitable for KDE and K-functions.



2.7 Ethical/usage notes

ACRA data contains entity names (public corporate info), not personal data.

Results are aggregated for planning insights; avoid singling out individual firms.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3
text:
A spatio-temporal point process (also called space-time or spatial-temporal point process) is a random collection of points, where each point represents the time and location of an event. Examples of events include incidence of disease, sightings or births of a species, or the occurrences of fires, earthquakes, lightning strikes, tsunamis, or volcanic eruptions.
The analysis of spatio-temporal point patterns is becoming increasingly necessary, given the rapid emergence of geographically and temporally indexed data in a wide range of fields. Several spatio-temporal point patterns analysis methods have been introduced and implemented in R in the last ten years. This chapter shows how various R packages can be combined to run a set of spatio-temporal point pattern analyses in a guided and intuitive way. A real world forest fire events in Kepulauan Bangka Belitung, Indonesia from 1st January 2023 to 31st December 2023 is used to illustrate the methods, procedures and interpretations.
The specific questions we would like to answer are:

Are the locations of forest fire in Kepulauan Bangka Belitung spatial and spatio-temporally independent?
If the answer is NO, where and when do the observed forest fire locations tend to cluster?

2 Data
For the purpose of this exercise, two data sets will be used, they are:

forestfires, a CSV file providing locations of forest fires detected from the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) sensor data.
The data are downloaded from Fire Information for Resource Management System.
Kepulauan_Bangka_Belitung, an ESRI shapefile showing the sub-district (i.e. kelurahan) boundary of Kepulauan Bangka Belitung.
The data set was downloaded from Indonesia Geospatial portal.
The original data covers the whole Indonesia. For the purpose of this exercise, only sub-districts within Kepulauan Bangka Belitung are extracted.

3 Installing and Loading the R packages
For the purpose of this study, six R packages will be used. They are:

sf – provides functions for importing, processing, and wrangling geospatial data.
raster – for handling raster data in R.
spatstat – for performing Spatial Point Patterns Analysis such as Kcross, Lcross, etc.
sparr – provides functions to estimate fixed and adaptive kernel-smoothed spatial relative risk surfaces via the density-ratio method and perform subsequent inference. Fixed-bandwidth spatiotemporal density and relative risk estimation is also supported.
tmap – provides functions to produce cartographic quality thematic maps.
tidyverse – a family of R packages that provide functions to perform common data science tasks including, but not limited to, data import, data transformation, data wrangling, and data visualisation.

2.6 Geoprocessing with sf package
Besides providing functions to handling (i.e. importing, exporting, assigning projection, transforming projection etc) geospatial data, sf package also offers a wide range of geoprocessing (also known as GIS analysis) functions.

2.6.1 Use case 1: Land acquisition analysis

2.6.1.1 The scenario
The authority is planning to upgrade the exiting cycling path. To do so, they need to acquire 5 metres of reserved land on the both sides of the existing cycling path. We are tasked to determine the extend of the land need to be acquired and their total area.


2.6.1.2 The Solution
To determine the extent of land needed for the cycling path upgrade, we first created 5-meter buffers around the existing cycling paths. After generating the buffers, we calculated their areas and then summed them up to obtain the total land involved in the acquisition, which amounted to 3,561,648 square metres.
To better understand the distribution of the required land, we focused on a specific case in the Tampines West planning subzone. We filtered out this subzone from the master plan and clipped the cycling path buffers within its boundaries. Finally, we plotted the results to visualize the buffered cycling paths inside Tampines West.

# 1. Create 5m buffer around cycling paths
buffer_cycling <- st_buffer(cyclingpath, dist = 5, nQuadSegs = 30)

# 2. Calculate buffer area
buffer_cycling <- buffer_cycling %>%
  mutate(AREA = st_area(geometry))

# 3. Total area of land to be acquired
total_area <- sum(buffer_cycling$AREA)
print(total_area)

3561648 [m^2]

# 4. Select Tampines West subzone
mpsz_selected <- mpsz %>%
  filter(SUBZONE_N == "TAMPINES WEST")

#transformation
buffer_cycling <- st_transform(buffer_cycling, st_crs(mpsz))


# 5. Clip buffer within Tampines West subzone
buffer_cycling_selected <- st_intersection(buffer_cycling, mpsz_selected)

# 6. Plot results
plot(st_geometry(mpsz_selected), main = "Cycling Path Buffer in Tampines West")
plot(st_geometry(buffer_cycling_selected), col = "lightblue", add = TRUE)
plot(st_geometry(cyclingpath), col = "red", lwd = 2, add = TRUE)

3 Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
###Overview In general, thematic mapping involves the use of map symbols to visualize selected properties of geographic features that are not naturally visible, such as population, temperature, crime rate, and property prices, just to mention a few of them.
Geovisualisation, on the other hand, is the process of using visual representations and cartographic techniques to explore, analyze, and communicate geospatial data. It combines elements of cartography, computer science, and information visualization to enhance spatial understanding and knowledge discovery.

3.1 Getting Started
In this hands-on exercise, the key R package used is tmap in R.
Besides tmap, five other R packages will be used. They are:

readr for importing delimited text files,

tidyr for tidying data,

dplyr for wrangling data,

sf for handling geospatial data, and

rvest for scraping (or harvesting) data from web pages.

Among the five packages, readr, tidyr, and dplyr are part of the tidyverse package.
The code chunk below will be used to install and load these packages in RStudio.

pacman::p_load(sf, tmap, tidyverse, rvest)

3.2.1.1 Tidying data
Function to extract values from the HTML description

extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) {
  if (is.na(html_text) || html_text == "") return(NA_character_)
  
  page <- read_html(html_text)
  rows <- page %>% html_elements("tr")
  
  value <- rows %>%
    keep(~ html_text2(html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>%
    html_element("td") %>%
    html_text2()
  
  if (length(value) == 0) NA_character_ else value
}


mpsz <- mpsz %>%

    PLN_AREA_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "PLN_AREA_N"),
    SUBZONE_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_N"),
    SUBZONE_C = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_C")
  ) %>%
  select(-Name, -Description) %>%

3.2.2 Importing Attribute Data into R
Next, we will be importing the respopagesextod2024.csv file into RStudio and saving it as a tibble dataframe called popdata.
We will perform this task by using the read_csv() function from the readr package, as shown in the code chunk below.

popdata <- readr::read_csv("C:/govanzz/ISSS626_GEO_AUG_2025/Hands-on_Ex/Hands-on_Ex01/data/aspatial/respopagesextod2024.csv")


3.2.2.1 Data Preparation

3.2.2.1.1 Data wrangling
The following data wrangling and transformation functions will be used:

pivot_wider() of tidyr package, and
mutate(), filter(), group_by() and select() of dplyr package


popdata2024 <- popdata %>%
  group_by(PA, SZ, AG) %>%
  summarise(`POP` = sum(`Pop`)) %>%
  ungroup()%>%
  pivot_wider(names_from=AG, 
              values_from=POP) %>%
  mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(.[3:6])
         +rowSums(.[12])) %>%
mutate(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` = rowSums(.[7:11])+
rowSums(.[13:15]))%>%
mutate(`AGED`=rowSums(.[16:21])) %>%
mutate(`TOTAL`=rowSums(.[3:21])) %>%  
mutate(`DEPENDENCY` = (`YOUNG` + `AGED`)
/`ECONOMY ACTIVE`) %>%
  select(`PA`, `SZ`, `YOUNG`, 
       `ECONOMY ACTIVE`, `AGED`, 
       `TOTAL`, `DEPENDENCY`)



3.2.2.1.2 Joining the attribute data and geospatial data
Before we can perform the georelational join, one extra step is required to convert the values in PA and SZ fields to uppercase. This is because the values of PA and SZ fields are made up of upper- and lowercase. On the other, hand the SUBZONE_N and PLN_AREA_N are in uppercase.

# 1. Clean and filter popdata2024
popdata2024 <- popdata2024 %>%
  mutate_at(.vars = vars(PA, SZ),
            .funs = list(toupper)) %>%
  filter(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` > 0)

# 2. Join with subzone boundaries
mpsz_pop2024 <- left_join(mpsz, popdata2024,
                          by = c("SUBZONE_N" = "SZ"))

# 3. Save the result
write_rds(mpsz_pop2024,
          "C:/govanzz/ISSS626_GEO_AUG_2025/Hands-on_Ex/Hands-on_Ex01/data/rds/mpsz_pop2024.rds")






3.3 Choropleth Mapping Geospatial Data Using tmap
Two approaches can be used to prepare thematic map using tmap, they are:

Plotting a thematic map quickly by using qtm().
Plotting highly customisable thematic map by using tmap elements.


3.3.1 Plotting a choropleth map quickly by using qtm()
The easiest and quickest to draw a choropleth map using tmap is using qtm(). It is concise and provides a good default visualisation in many cases.
The code chunk below will draw a cartographic standard choropleth map as shown below.

tmap_mode("plot")
qtm(shp = mpsz_pop2024, 
    fill = "DEPENDENCY")








Things to learn from the code chunk above:

tmap_mode() with “plot” option is used to produce a static map. For interactive mode, “view” option should be used.
fill argument is used to map the attribute (i.e. DEPENDENCY)



3.3.2 Creating a choropleth map by using tmap’s elements
Despite its usefulness of drawing a choropleth map quickly and easily, the disadvantge of qtm() is that it makes aesthetics of individual layers harder to control. To draw a high quality cartographic choropleth map as shown in the figure below, tmap’s drawing elements should be used.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile", 
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by planning subzone") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha =0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: Planning Sub-zone boundary from Urban Redevelopment Authorithy (URA)\n and Population data from Department of Statistics DOS", 
             position = c("left", "bottom"))








In the following sub-section, we will share with you tmap functions that used to plot these elements. ##### Drawing a base map The basic building block of tmap is tm_shape() followed by one or more layer elemments such as tm_polygons(), tm_symbols(), tm_lines(), tm_raster() and tm_text().
In the code chunk below, tm_shape() is used to define the input data (i.e mpsz_pop2024) and tm_polygons() is used to draw the planning subzone polygons

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons()









3.3.2.1 Drawing a choropleth map using tm_polygons()
To draw a choropleth map showing the geographical distribution of a selected variable by planning subzone, we just need to assign the target variable such as Dependency to tm_polygons().

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY")










3.3.2.2 Drawing a choropleth map using tm_fill() and tm_border()
Actually, tm_polygons() is a wraper of tm_fill() and tm_border(). tm_fill() shades the polygons by using the default colour scheme and tm_borders() adds the borders of the polygon features onto the choropleth map.
The code chunk below draws a choropleth map by using tm_fill() alone.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY")








To add the boundary of the planning subzones, tm_borders() will be used as shown in the code chunk below.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders()








Notice that light-gray border lines have been added on the choropleth map.
The fill_alpha argument is used to define transparency number between 0 (totally transparent) and 1 (not transparent). By default, the alpha value of the col is used (normally 1).
Beside fill_alpha argument, there are three other arguments for tm_borders(), they are:

col = border colour,
lwd = border line width. The default is 1, and
lty = border line type. The default is “solid”.


tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders(col = "grey60",
             lwd = 0.1,
             lty = "dashed")











3.3.3 Data classification methods of tmap
Most choropleth maps employ some methods of data classification. The point of classification is to take a large number of observations and group them into data ranges or classes.
tmap provides a total ten data classification methods, namely: fixed, sd, equal, pretty (default), quantile, kmeans, hclust, bclust, fisher, and jenks.
To define a data classification method, the style argument of tm_fill() or tm_polygons() will be used.

3.3.3.1 Plotting choropleth maps with built-in classification methods
The code chunk below shows a quantile data classification that used 5 classes.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








In the code chunk below, equal data classification method is used.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "equal",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)









tmap_mode("plot")

# Helper to build one choropleth with chosen style + classes
make_map <- function(style = "quantile", n = 5, title = NULL) {
  tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
    tm_polygons(
      fill = "DEPENDENCY",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = style, n = n, values = "brewer.blues"),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(title = title %||% paste0("Style: ", style, " (n=", n, ")"))
    ) +
    tm_borders(col = "grey40", lwd = 0.3, fill_alpha = 0.5) +
    tm_layout(frame = TRUE)
}

# ---------- DIY 1: Compare classification methods ----------
map_quantile <- make_map("quantile", 5, "Quantile (n=5)")
map_equal    <- make_map("equal",    5, "Equal (n=5)")
map_pretty   <- make_map("pretty",   5, "Pretty (n=5)")
map_jenks    <- make_map("jenks",    5, "Jenks (n=5)")
map_kmeans   <- make_map("kmeans",   5, "K-means (n=5)")

tmap_arrange(map_quantile, map_equal, map_pretty, map_jenks, map_kmeans, nrow = 2)







# ---------- DIY 2: Same method, different numbers of classes ----------
q2  <- make_map("quantile", 2,  "Quantile (n=2)")
q6  <- make_map("quantile", 6,  "Quantile (n=6)")
q10 <- make_map("quantile", 10, "Quantile (n=10)")
q20 <- make_map("quantile", 20, "Quantile (n=20)")

tmap_arrange(q2, q6, q10, q20, nrow = 2)









Different classification methods change how patterns are revealed:

Quantile shows relative ranking clearly but can split similar values.

Equal bins exaggerate extremes when data are skewed.

Jenks and K-means highlight natural clusters more effectively.

The number of classes affects readability:

Few classes (2–4) oversimplify the data and hide variation.

Moderate classes (5–7) balance detail and clarity — best for reporting.

Many classes (10–20) make the map cluttered and hard to interpret.

For communication and decision-making, Jenks or Quantile with ~5–7 classes gives the clearest insights.



3.3.3.2 Plotting choropleth map with custome break
For all the built-in styles, the category breaks are computed internally. In order to override these defaults, the breakpoints can be set explicitly by means of the breaks argument to the tm_scale_intervals(). It is important to note that, in tmap the breaks include a minimum and maximum. As a result, in order to end up with n categories, n+1 elements must be specified in the breaks option (the values must be in increasing order).
Code chunk below will be used to compute and display the descriptive statistics of DEPENDENCY field.

summary(mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
 0.1905  0.7450  0.8377  0.8738  0.9366 12.7500      94 


With reference to the results above, we set break point at 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, and 0.90. In addition, we also need to include a minimum and maximum, which we set at 0 and 100. Our breaks vector is thus c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00)
Now, we will plot the choropleth map by using the code chunk below.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00))) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)











3.3.4 Colour Scheme
tmap supports colour ramps either defined by the user or a set of predefined colour ramps from the RColorBrewer package.

3.3.4.1 Using ColourBrewer palette
To change the colour, we assign the preferred colour to palette argument of values as shown in the code chunk below.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








Notice that the choropleth map is shaded in green.
To reverse the colour shading, add a “-” prefix.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "-brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)










3.3.4.2 Cartographic Furniture
Beside map style, tmap also also provides arguments to draw other map furniture such as compass, scale bar and grid lines.
In the code chunk below, tm_compass(), tm_scale_bar(), tm_grid() and tm_credit() are used to add compass, scale bar, grid lines and data sources onto the choropleth map.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(lwd = 0.1, alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: data.gov.sg & singstat",
             position = c("left", "bottom"))











3.3.5 Map Layout
Map layout refers to the combination of all map elements into a cohensive map. It includes the map background, frame, typography, scale, aspect ratio, margins, and more.
We can customize the map layout using the tm_layout() function.

3.3.5.1 Map Legend
In tmap, several legend options are provided to change the placement, format and appearance of the legend.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_pos_auto_in() +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(lwd = 0.1, alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: data.gov.sg & singstat",
             position = c("left", "bottom"))










3.3.5.2 Map Style
tmap allows a wide variety of layout settings to be changed. They can be called by using tmap_style().
The code chunk below shows the classic style is used.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "-brewer.greens")) + 
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) + 
  tmap_style("natural")








To reset use the code below

tmap_style("white")





3.4 Drawing Small Multiple Choropleth Maps
Small multiple maps, also referred to as facet maps, are composed of many maps arrange side-by-side, and sometimes stacked vertically. Small multiple maps enable the visualisation of how spatial relationships change with respect to another variable, such as time.
In tmap, small multiple maps can be plotted in three ways:

by assigning multiple values to at least one of the asthetic arguments,
by creating multiple stand-alone maps with tmap_arrange(), and
by defining a group-by variable in tm_facets().


3.4.1 By assigning multiple values to at least one of the aesthetic arguments
In this example, small multiple choropleth maps are created by assigning two variables to the visual variable (i.e. fill).

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) + 
  tm_polygons(
    fill = c("YOUNG", "AGED"),
    fill.legend = 
      tm_legend(position = tm_pos_in(
        "right", "bottom")),
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "equal", 
      n = 5,
      values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tmap_style("natural")









3.4.1.1 By arrange multiples choropleth maps in a grid layout
In this example, multiple choropleth maps are created and tmap_arrnage() is used to arrnage them in a grid layout.

youngmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+ 
  tm_polygons(fill = "YOUNG",
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = tm_pos_in(
                  "right", "bottom"),
                  item.height = 0.8),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile", 
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of young population")
                
agedmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+ 
  tm_polygons(fill = "AGED",
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = tm_pos_in(
                  "right", "bottom"),
                item.height = 0.8),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
              style = "quantile", 
              values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of aged population")

tmap_arrange(youngmap, agedmap, asp=1, ncol=2)











3.4.2 By defining a group-by variable in tm_facets()
In this example, multiple small choropleth maps are created by using tm_facets().

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_fill(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
            style = "quantile",
            values = "brewer.blues")) + 
  tm_facets(by = "REGION_N",
            nrow = 2, 
            ncols = 3,
            free.coords=TRUE, 
            drop.units=TRUE) +
  tm_layout(legend.show = TRUE,
            title.position = c("center", "center"), 
            title.size = 20) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)











3.5 Mappping Spatial Object Meeting a Selection Criterion
Instead of creating small multiple choropleth map, you can also use filter() of dplyr package to select geographical area of interest and plot a choropleth map focus only on the selected region.

mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION") %>%
  tm_shape() +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile", 
                values = "brewer.greens"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend()) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)










3.6 Complementing Thematic Map with Statistical Chart
Maps and statistical charts complement each other by visually representing different aspects of the same data, offering a more comprehensive understanding. Maps excel at showing spatial relationships and geographical patterns, while charts effectively display numerical data, trends, and comparisons. Combining both allows for a more insightful and engaging data narrative, especially when dealing with spatial data that also has quantifiable characteristics.
With tmap, statistical chart and be incorporate into the map visualisation by using fill.chat argument of map layers and legend chart feature as shown in the code chunk below.

mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION") %>%
  tm_shape() +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile", 
                values = "brewer.greens"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(),
              fill.chart = tm_chart_box()) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_layout(asp = 0.8)








In the code chunk below, We improve the visual representation further by highlighting and lebaling the outliers on the choropleth map.

mpsz_selected <- mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION")

stats <- boxplot.stats(mpsz_selected$DEPENDENCY)

outlier_vals <- stats$out

outlier_sf <- mpsz_selected[mpsz_selected$DEPENDENCY %in% outlier_vals, ]

tm_shape(mpsz_selected) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
            style = "quantile", 
            values = "brewer.blues"),
          fill.legend = tm_legend(),
          fill.chart = tm_chart_box()) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
tm_shape(outlier_sf) +
  tm_borders(col = "red", lwd = 2) +
  tm_text("SUBZONE_N", col = "red", size = 0.7) +
  tm_layout(asp = 0.8)










3.7 Creating Interactive Maps
Interactive maps let users actively explore and interact with the data they display. Unlike static maps, you can zoom in and out, pan across areas, click on locations for more information, and even work with data overlays or visualizations—making the experience more dynamic and informative. One of the great things about tmap is that it lets you switch easily between static and interactive maps using tmap_mode(), so you can choose the view that best suits your analysis.
By modifying the code chunk in sub-section 3.5, the code chunks below build an interactive map using

region_selected <- mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION")
region_bbox <- st_bbox(region_selected)

stats <- boxplot.stats(region_selected$DEPENDENCY)
outlier_vals <- stats$out
outlier_sf <- region_selected[region_selected$DEPENDENCY %in% outlier_vals, ]

tmap_mode("view")
tm_shape(region_selected, 
         bbox = region_bbox) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          id = "SUBZONE_N",
          popup.vars = c(
            "Name" = "SUBZONE_N", 
            "Dependency" = "DEPENDENCY")) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_shape(outlier_sf) +
  tm_borders(col = "red", lwd = 2)







tmap_mode("plot")

The interactive map above is far from satisfactory. While we want to encourage users to engage and explore the interactive by zooming in and out of the study area freely. But, users might lost in the cyberspace with too much freedom to zoom-in and zoom-out.
To address this issue, set_zoom_limits argument can be used to limit the map extend users can zooming in and out of the map areas as shown below.

region_selected <- mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION")
region_bbox <- st_bbox(region_selected)

stats <- boxplot.stats(region_selected$DEPENDENCY)
outlier_vals <- stats$out
outlier_sf <- region_selected[region_selected$DEPENDENCY %in% outlier_vals, ]

tmap_mode("view")

tm_shape(region_selected, 
         bbox = region_bbox) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          id = "SUBZONE_N",
          popup.vars = c(
            "Name" = "SUBZONE_N", 
            "Dependency" = "DEPENDENCY")) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_shape(outlier_sf) +
  tm_borders(col = "red", lwd = 2) +
  tm_view(set_zoom_limits = c(12,14))





tmap_mode("plot")

Spatial Point Pattern Analysis (SPPA) is the evaluation of the pattern or distribution of a set of points on a surface. The points may represent:

Events such as crimes, traffic accidents, or disease onsets, or

Business services (e.g., coffee shops and fast-food outlets) or facilities such as childcare centres and eldercare centres.

First-order Spatial Point Pattern Analysis (1st-SPPA) focuses on understanding the intensity or density of points across a study area. It examines how the distribution of points varies over space, essentially identifying trends or patterns in point density. This type of analysis deals with the individual locations of points and their distribution, without considering interactions between them.
Second-order spatial point pattern analysis examines the relationships between points, studying whether they are clustered, dispersed, or randomly distributed using tools like Ripley’s K function or nearest-neighbor analysis. It answers the question: “How do points interact with each other in space?”

1 First Order Spatial Point Pattern Analysis
In essence, 1st-SPPA helps answer questions such as:

Where are points most densely located within the study area?

Is point density uniform, or does it vary across space?

How spread out is the point pattern?

In this chapter, we will gain hands-on experience with spatstat to perform two commonly used 1st-SPPA methods.
The specific questions we would like to answer are as follows:

Are the childcare centres in Singapore randomly distributed throughout the country?

If the answer is not, then the next logical question is: where are the locations with higher concentration of childcare centres?


1.1 The Data
Child Care Services data from data.gov.sg, a point feature data providing both location and attribute information of childcare centres. Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (No Sea), a polygon feature data providing information of URA 2019 Master Plan Planning Subzone boundary data.
geojson format were used


1.2 Installing and Loading the R packages
In this hands-on exercise, we will use five R packages:

sf: A modern package designed to import, manage, and process vector-based geospatial data in R.

spatstat: A powerful package for point pattern analysis. We will use it to perform 1st- and 2nd-order spatial point pattern analysis and derive kernel density estimation (KDE) layers.

terra: A fast and efficient package for working with raster and vector data, designed to replace the older raster package. In our exercise, we will use it to convert image outputs generated by spatstat into terra format.

tmap: A package for creating cartographic-quality static maps and interactive maps (via the leaflet API).

rvest: A package for web scraping, which we can use to harvest data directly from web pages.

We will install and load these packages using the following code:

               tmap, rvest, tidyverse)

1.5 Clark-Evan Test for Nearest Neighbour Analysis
Nearest Neighbor Analysis (NNA) is a spatial statistics method that calculates the average distance between each point and its closest neighbor to determine if a pattern of points is clustered, dispersed, or randomly distributed.
Clark-Evans test is a specific statistical method used within NNA to quantify whether a point pattern is clustered, random, or uniformly spaced, using the Clark-Evans aggregation index (R) to describe this pattern. NNA provides a numerical value that describes the degree of clustering or regularity, and the Clark-Evans test calculates a specific index (R) for this purpose
In this section, we will perform the Clark-Evans test of aggregation for a spatial point pattern by using [clarkevans.test()] from the spatstat.explore package.
The test hypotheses are:

H₀: The distribution of childcare services is randomly distributed.

H₁: The distribution of childcare services is not randomly distributed.

We will use a 95% confidence interval for this test.

1.5.1 Perform the Clark-Evans test without CSR
clarkevans.test() of spatstat.explore package support two Clark-Evans test, namely: without CRS and with CRS. In the code chunk below, Clark-Evans test without CSR method is used.

clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,
                correction="none",
                clipregion="sg_owin",
                alternative=c("clustered"))

    No edge correction
    Z-test

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.49444, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)


Statistical Conclusion:
From the Clark-Evans test, the observed R value is 0.53532 with a p-value < 2.2e-16.
Since the p-value is far below 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis of complete spatial randomness.
The result supports the alternative hypothesis that childcare services are clustered rather than randomly distributed.
Business Communication:
Based on this analysis, we conclude that childcare centres in Singapore tend to be located in clusters.
This clustering likely reflects demand-driven planning (e.g., centres opening in areas with higher child populations) or zoning policies.
For decision-makers, this indicates that underserved areas may exist where childcare services are sparse, highlighting opportunities for policy adjustments or business expansion into less-served neighborhoods.



1.6 Kernel Density Estimation Method
Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) is a valuable tool for visualising and analyzing first-order spatial point patterns. It is widely considered a method within Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis (ESDA) because it’s used to visualize and understand spatial data patterns by transforms discrete point data (like locations of childcare service, crime incidents or disease cases) into continuous density surfaces that reveal clusters and variations in event occurrences, without making prior assumptions about data distribution. It helps to begin understanding data distribution, identify hotspots, and explore relationships between spatial variables before performing more rigorous analysis.
In this section, you will learn how to compute the kernel density estimation (KDE) of childcare services in Singapore.

1.6.1 Working with automatic bandwidth selection method
The code chunk below computes a kernel density by using the following configurations of [density()] from spatstat:

Other recommended methods are [bw.CvL()], [bw.scott()], or [bw.ppl()].

The smoothing kernel used is gaussian (default).
Other smoothing methods include: "epanechnikov", "quartic", or "disc".

The intensity estimate can be corrected for edge effect bias using the method described by Jones (1993) and Diggle (2010, equation 18.9).
The default is FALSE.

  sigma=bw.diggle,

extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) {
  if (is.na(html_text) || html_text == "") return(NA_character_)
  
  page <- read_html(html_text)
  rows <- page %>% html_elements("tr")
  
  value <- rows %>%
    keep(~ html_text2(html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>%
    html_element("td") %>%
    html_text2()
  
  if (length(value) == 0) NA_character_ else value
}

2 2nd Order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods
Second-order spatial point pattern analysis examines the spatial relationships between points in a pattern, specifically focusing on how the presence of one point influences the location of others. It goes beyond simply describing the overall density of points (first-order effects) by investigating clustering, dispersion, or randomness at various spatial scales.
Using appropriate functions of spatstat, this hands-on exercise aims to discover the spatial point processes of childcare centres in Singapore.
The specific questions we would like to answer are as follows:

Are the childcare centres in Singapore randomly distributed throughout the country?

If the answer is not, then the next logical question is: where are the locations with higher concentration of childcare centres? ### Data

5 Computing Contiguity Spatial Weights
In this section, we will learn how to use poly2nb() from the spdep package to compute contiguity weight matrices for the study area.
This function builds a neighbours list based on regions with contiguous boundaries.
The queen argument controls the contiguity rule:
queen = TRUE (default): Uses Queen contiguity — regions are considered neighbours if they share at least one point (edge or corner).
queen = FALSE: Uses Rook contiguity — regions are considered neighbours only if they share a common edge.
If we do not specify this argument, the default is queen = TRUE, meaning the function will return a list of first-order neighbours using the Queen criteria.

5.1 Computing (QUEEN) contiguity based neighbours
The code chunk below is used to compute Queen contiguity weight matrix.

wm_q <- poly2nb(hunan, queen=TRUE)

6 Computing distance based neighbours
In this section, we will learn how to derive distance-based weight matrices by using dnearneigh() from the spdep package. The function identifies neighbours of region points by Euclidean distance within a distance band, where the lower bound is controlled by d1= and the upper bound by d2=. If unprojected coordinates are used and either specified in the coordinates object x or provided as a two-column matrix with longlat = TRUE, then great-circle distances in kilometers will be calculated, assuming the WGS84 reference ellipsoid.

6.1 Determine the cut-off distance
Firstly, we need to determine the upper limit for distance band by using the steps below:

Return a matrix with the indices of points belonging to the set of the k nearest neighbours of each other by using knearneigh() of spdep.
Convert the knn object returned by knearneigh() into a neighbours list of class nb with a list of integer vectors containing neighbour region number ids by using knn2nb().
Return the length of neighbour relationship edges by using nbdists() of spdep. The function returns in the units of the coordinates if the coordinates are projected, in km otherwise.
Remove the list structure of the returned object by using unlist().


#coords <- coordinates(hunan)
k1 <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords))
k1dists <- unlist(nbdists(k1, coords, longlat = TRUE))
summary(k1dists)

8 Row-standardised Weights Matrix
Next, we need to assign weights to each neighboring polygon. In our case, each neighboring polygon will be assigned equal weight (style=“W”). This is accomplished by assigning the fraction 1/(#ofneighbors) to each neighboring county then summing the weighted income values. While this is the most intuitive way to summaries the neighbors’ values it has one drawback in that polygons along the edges of the study area will base their lagged values on fewer polygons thus potentially over- or under-estimating the true nature of the spatial autocorrelation in the data. For this example, we’ll stick with the style=“W” option for simplicity’s sake but note that other more robust options are available, notably style=“B”.

section: Building an interative plot with ggplotly
text:
Building an interative plot with ggplotly
The previous code chunks uses plot() to visualise the envelopes of the second-order summary statistics (such as L-function). The output is a static plot, therefore it can be difficult to make accurate guesstimates of the statistics and the corresponding distance, r.
The below code chunk converts the output (which is in a list form) into a dataframe, which can be used to generate a similar plot using appropriate aesthetic mappings from ggplot package. Finally, ggplotly() is used to convert the ggplot into an interactive plotly visualisation.
The codes were referenced from a R-blogger article. Further modifications were made to enhance the user experience by customizing the tooltips for greater clarity and intuition.

title <- "Pairwise Distance: L function"

Lcsr_df <- as.data.frame(L_tm.csr)

colour=c("#0D657D","#ee770d","#D3D3D3")
csr_plot <- ggplot(Lcsr_df, aes(r, obs-r))+
  # plot observed value
  geom_line(colour=c("#4d4d4d"))+
  geom_line(aes(r,theo-r), colour="red", linetype = "dashed")+
  # plot simulation envelopes
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin=lo-r,ymax=hi-r),alpha=0.1, colour=c("#91bfdb")) +
  xlab("Distance r (m)") +
  ylab("L(r)-r") +
  geom_rug(data=Lcsr_df[Lcsr_df$obs > Lcsr_df$hi,], sides="b", colour=colour[1])  +
  geom_rug(data=Lcsr_df[Lcsr_df$obs < Lcsr_df$lo,], sides="b", colour=colour[2]) +
  geom_rug(data=Lcsr_df[Lcsr_df$obs >= Lcsr_df$lo & Lcsr_df$obs <= Lcsr_df$hi,], sides="b", color=colour[3]) +
  theme_tufte()+
  ggtitle(title)

text1<-"Significant clustering"
text2<-"Significant segregation"
text3<-"Not significant clustering/segregation"

# the below conditional statement is required to ensure that the labels (text1/2/3) are assigned to the correct traces
if (nrow(Lcsr_df[Lcsr_df$obs > Lcsr_df$hi,])==0){ 
  if (nrow(Lcsr_df[Lcsr_df$obs < Lcsr_df$lo,])==0){ 
    ggplotly(csr_plot, dynamicTicks=T) %>%
      style(text = text3, traces = 4) %>%
      rangeslider() 
  }else if (nrow(Lcsr_df[Lcsr_df$obs >= Lcsr_df$lo & Lcsr_df$obs <= Lcsr_df$hi,])==0){ 
    ggplotly(csr_plot, dynamicTicks=T) %>%
      style(text = text2, traces = 4) %>%
      rangeslider() 
  }else {
    ggplotly(csr_plot, dynamicTicks=T) %>%
      style(text = text2, traces = 4) %>%
      style(text = text3, traces = 5) %>%
      rangeslider() 
  }
} else if (nrow(Lcsr_df[Lcsr_df$obs < Lcsr_df$lo,])==0){
  if (nrow(Lcsr_df[Lcsr_df$obs >= Lcsr_df$lo & Lcsr_df$obs <= Lcsr_df$hi,])==0){
    ggplotly(csr_plot, dynamicTicks=T) %>%
      style(text = text1, traces = 4) %>%
      rangeslider() 
  } else{
    ggplotly(csr_plot, dynamicTicks=T) %>%
      style(text = text1, traces = 4) %>%
      style(text = text3, traces = 5) %>%
      rangeslider()
  }
} else{
  ggplotly(csr_plot, dynamicTicks=T) %>%
    style(text = text1, traces = 4) %>%
    style(text = text2, traces = 5) %>%
    style(text = text3, traces = 6) %>%
    rangeslider()
  }











Note



The main features of the above visualisation:

The observed and theoretical values of L(r)-r (including the upper and lower curves of the simulated envelope) can be found in the tooltip upon hovering the cursor over the geometry layers.
The range slider below the plot enables users to pan and zoom in to a specific range of distance.
The colored bands at the bottom of the line graph gives a clearer indication of significant or insignificant spatial segregation/ clustering at distance r. Dark green bands indicate significant clustering, orange indicate significant segregation, while grey indicates insignificant clustering/segregation.
Tooltips were added to provide color legend information.

4 Data Wrangling

4.1 Preparing the Subzone Boundary (why & how)
This chunk converts URA’s Master Plan Subzone (No Sea) GeoJSON into a clean, projected GeoPackage with consistent field names. We use it as: 1) the analysis window for point-pattern methods, and
2) the join layer to aggregate new businesses by subzone/planning area. Extract data for planning

sz_raw_path <- "data/geospatial/MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaGEOJSON.geojson"

subzones <- st_read(sz_raw_path, quiet = TRUE) %>%
  clean_names() %>%                 # lower_case_names
  st_make_valid() %>%               # fix any tiny geometry issues
  st_transform(3414)                # SVY21 metres (needed for KDE/K-functions)

Standardise key attribute names
Cleaning & Standardizing URA Subzone Shapefile
This block extracts metadata fields from the HTML in the description column.
Helper function – extract_field()
- Uses regex to find the value of a field (key) inside HTML <th>…</th><td>…</td>.
- Returns a cleaned string; missing/empty values → NA_character_.
Standardize subzones (subzones_std)
- Applies mutate() to create clean columns from the HTML description:
- SUBZONE_NO, SUBZONE_N, SUBZONE_C
- CA_IND (planning area indicator)
- PLN_AREA_N, PLN_AREA_C
- REGION_N, REGION_C
- FMEL_UPD_D (last update date)
- Keeps only standardized fields + geometry.
- Ensures valid geometries (st_make_valid()).
- Transforms to EPSG:3414 (Singapore SVY21 / meters).
Export
- Saves cleaned dataset as a GeoPackage (mpsz_subzones_2019_nosea.gpkg) in data/geospatial/.
- Overwrites the subzones layer if it already exists (delete_dsn = TRUE).

# Helper: extract a field value from the HTML in `description`
extract_field <- function(html, key){
  m <- str_match(html, paste0("<th>", key, "</th>\\s*<td>([^<]*)</td>"))
  val <- m[, 2]
  val <- ifelse(is.na(val) | val == "", NA_character_, str_squish(val))
  return(val)
}

subzones_std <- subzones %>%
  mutate(
    SUBZONE_NO = as.integer(extract_field(description, "SUBZONE_NO")),
    SUBZONE_N  = extract_field(description, "SUBZONE_N"),
    SUBZONE_C  = extract_field(description, "SUBZONE_C"),
    CA_IND     = extract_field(description, "CA_IND"),
    PLN_AREA_N = extract_field(description, "PLN_AREA_N"),
    PLN_AREA_C = extract_field(description, "PLN_AREA_C"),
    REGION_N   = extract_field(description, "REGION_N"),
    REGION_C   = extract_field(description, "REGION_C"),
    FMEL_UPD_D = extract_field(description, "FMEL_UPD_D")
  ) %>%
  select(SUBZONE_NO, SUBZONE_N, SUBZONE_C, CA_IND,
         PLN_AREA_N, PLN_AREA_C, REGION_N, REGION_C, FMEL_UPD_D, geometry) %>%
  st_make_valid() %>%
  st_transform(3414)

# save a clean, fast-to-load copy
st_write(subzones_std, "data/geospatial/mpsz_subzones_2019_nosea.gpkg",
         layer = "subzones", delete_dsn = TRUE)

4.2 Load & Tidy Acra
This code chunk loads and cleans ACRA business registration data for analysis.

File setup

Defines input/output directories (aspatial_dir, rds_dir), ensures RDS folder exists.

Lists all ACRA CSV files in data/aspatial matching the pattern ACRA*.csv.

Load raw data

Reads all CSVs into one dataframe with map_dfr().

Applies clean_names() to standardize column names (snake_case).

Tidy & transform

Converts registration_incorporation_date into proper Date (reg_date).

Derives year, month number, and labelled month.

Cleans postal_code: keeps only digits, pads to 6 digits (left-padded with 0s).

Normalises primary_ssic_code: ensures 5-character format (padded with 0s).

Extracts ssic2 (2-digit) and ssic3 (3-digit) industry prefixes.

Filter study window

Keeps only records with valid reg_date between 1 Jan 2024 and 30 Jun 2025.



aspatial_dir <- "data/aspatial"
rds_dir      <- "data/rds"
dir.create(rds_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
file_list <- list.files(aspatial_dir, pattern = "^ACRA.*\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)

acra_raw <- file_list |>
  map_dfr(~ read_csv(.x, show_col_types = FALSE)) |>
  clean_names()

# 2) Tidy dates, SSIC, postal codes; derive time fields; filter study window
acra_tidy <- acra_raw |>
  mutate(
    reg_date  = as.Date(registration_incorporation_date),
    year      = year(reg_date),
    month_num = month(reg_date),
    month     = month(reg_date, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE),

    # keep only digits in postal_code; left-pad to 6
    postal_code = postal_code |>
      str_replace_all("[^0-9]", "") |>
      str_pad(width = 6, side = "left", pad = "0"),

    # normalise primary SSIC to 5 chars, and derive 2-/3-digit prefixes
    primary_ssic_code = str_pad(str_sub(primary_ssic_code, 1, 5), 5, pad = "0"),
    ssic2 = str_sub(primary_ssic_code, 1, 2),
    ssic3 = str_sub(primary_ssic_code, 1, 3)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(reg_date),
         reg_date >= as.Date("2024-01-01"),
         reg_date <= as.Date("2025-06-30"))



4.3 Select the 3 Industries
Choosing the three industries
The assignment requires at least three business types. We select broad, policy-relevant 2-digit SSIC groups that span consumer, knowledge, and logistics activities:

56 — Food & Beverage Service Activities (restaurants, cafés, bars)

62 — Computer programming, IT consultancy & related activities

52 — Warehousing & support activities for transportation

In the code below, we:

Build a small lookup to attach readable sector labels to each 2-digit SSIC.

Filter the cleaned ACRA records to these codes.

Produce a quick sector × year table to sanity-check sample sizes for 2024 and 2025.

4.4 Geocode unique postcodes with OneMap
This chunk defines a helper to geocode postal codes using the OneMap Singapore API and attach coordinates to business records.

Helper function onemap_lookup(pc)



Sends a GET request to OneMap’s API with a given postal code.

If a match is found:

Extracts postal code, X (longitude), Y (latitude).

Returns as a tibble.


If no match:

Returns postal code with NA for coordinates.



Geocode unique postcodes



Collects unique postal codes from biz_sel.

Loops with map_dfr(), calling onemap_lookup() for each.

Uses tryCatch() to handle API errors (returns NA if failure).

Produces geo_tbl, a lookup table of postal codes with coordinates.


Join back to businesses



Joins geo_tbl back to business dataset (biz_sel) using postal code as key.

Filters out rows where geocoding failed (NA X/Y).

Final output: biz_geo, a table of businesses with valid geocoded coordinates.


# Helper that hits OneMap Search API for one postcode
onemap_lookup <- function(pc){
  res <- GET("https://onemap.gov.sg/api/common/elastic/search",
             query = list(searchVal = pc, returnGeom = "Y", getAddrDetails = "Y", pageNum = "1"))
  js <- content(res)
  if (!is.null(js$found) && js$found > 0) {
    r <- js$results[[1]]

6 1st Order Spatio Temporal Analysis
Convert sf → owin and ppp

# Build polygonal window (country outline) from filtered subzones
W <- spatstat.geom::as.owin(st_union(subzones_use))   # SVY21 metres (EPSG:3414)

# Helper: convert an sf points subset to ppp in window W
to_ppp <- function(pts_sf) {
  xy <- sf::st_coordinates(pts_sf)
  spatstat.geom::ppp(x = xy[,1], y = xy[,2], window = W, check = FALSE)
}


6.1 Clark–Evans test per sector
The Clark–Evans nearest-neighbour test evaluates whether business registrations are randomly distributed, clustered, or regularly spaced relative to Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR).

Null hypothesis (H₀): The point pattern of business registrations follows CSR (i.e., randomly distributed).

Alternative hypothesis (H₁): The point pattern is more clustered than CSR (R < 1).

We test this hypothesis for each selected sector (F&B, IT, Logistics/Warehousing) using both the asymptotic test and the Monte Carlo CSR simulation (999 realisations).

sectors <- unique(biz_pts_use$sector)
# Asymptotic (no CSR simulation)
ce_asym <- lapply(sectors, function(sec){
  X <- to_ppp(biz_pts_use %>% filter(sector == sec))
  z <- clarkevans.test(X, correction = "none", clipregion = W, alternative = "clustered")
  tibble(sector = sec,
         n = X$n,
         R = unname(z$statistic),
         p_value = z$p.value,
         method = "Asymptotic (no CSR)")
}) %>% bind_rows()

# Monte Carlo against CSR (recommended for reporting)
set.seed(42)
ce_mc <- lapply(sectors, function(sec){
  X <- to_ppp(biz_pts_use %>% filter(sector == sec))
  z <- clarkevans.test(X, correction = "none", clipregion = W,
                       alternative = "clustered", method = "MonteCarlo", nsim = 999)
  tibble(sector = sec,
         n = X$n,
         R = unname(z$statistic),
         p_value = z$p.value,
         method = "Monte Carlo (999 CSR sims)")
}) %>% bind_rows()

ce_results <- bind_rows(ce_asym, ce_mc) %>%
  arrange(sector, method)
ce_results

Clark–Evans nearest-neighbour test (window = Singapore outline, SVY21).
Across all sectors the Clark–Evans statistic (R) is below 1 and Monte-Carlo p-values are significant (()), indicating clustering relative to CSR at nearest-neighbour scale.

IT (62): (R ), (p ) → strongest clustering. Likely reflects CBD/fringe-CBD registered-office addresses and business-park nodes (one-north, CBP).

2) using K/CSR envelopes to see at which spatial ranges clustering persists beyond nearest neighbours.


6.2 Spatial Intensity of F&B (SSIC 56) Business Registrations
In this section, we compute and visualize the spatial intensity of F&B (SSIC 56) business registrations:

Cache paths


Create folders (data/rds, data/rasters) to store intermediate results.

This avoids re-running expensive computations every time the document is rendered.


Data preparation


F&B points are filtered from the master dataset (biz_pts_use).

Their coordinates are extracted and converted into a ppp object (planar point pattern) using spatstat.

The observation window W is already defined from the trimmed planning area polygons.


Kernel Density Estimation (KDE)


If a cached result exists, it is loaded.

Otherwise, a suitable bandwidth is estimated with bw.diggle, with safeguards (clamped between 300 m and 800 m).

The KDE is then computed using a Gaussian kernel.

The result is saved as an .rds file for future use.


Scaling and conversion


The density is originally in units of points per m².

Multiply by 1e6 to rescale into points per km², a more interpretable measure.

Convert the raster into a SpatRaster with the correct CRS (EPSG:3414).


Saving outputs


Save the raster as a GeoTIFF (.tif) so it can be reused in GIS software.


Mapping


Using tmap, render a choropleth of F&B intensity.

Overlay planning area boundaries (thin white borders) and the outer municipal boundary (thicker black border).

The legend title clearly states that values represent registrations per km².


# --- Always-available constants (paths) ---
rds_dir      <- "data/rds"
rasters_dir  <- "data/rasters"
dir.create(rds_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(rasters_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

fnb_kde_rds <- file.path(rds_dir, "fnb_kde_im.rds")
fnb_bw_rds  <- file.path(rds_dir, "fnb_bw.rds")
fnb_kde_tif <- file.path(rasters_dir, "fnb_kde_per_km2.tif")

# --- Ensure window and ppp exist (robust to earlier chunks being skipped) ---
if (!exists("subzones_use")) stop("subzones_use is missing; load/build it before this chunk.")
if (!exists("W")) {
  W <- spatstat.geom::as.owin(sf::st_union(subzones_use))
}
if (!exists("biz_pts_use")) stop("biz_pts_use is missing; load/build it before this chunk.")

fnb_sf  <- dplyr::filter(biz_pts_use, sector == "F&B (56)")
xy      <- sf::st_coordinates(fnb_sf)
fnb_ppp <- spatstat.geom::ppp(x = xy[,1], y = xy[,2], window = W, check = FALSE)

# --- Load or compute KDE + bandwidth, and persist both ---
fnb_bw <- NA_real_
kde_im <- NULL

if (file.exists(fnb_kde_rds)) {
  kde_im <- readRDS(fnb_kde_rds)
  if (file.exists(fnb_bw_rds)) fnb_bw <- readRDS(fnb_bw_rds)
}

if (is.null(kde_im) || !is.numeric(fnb_bw) || is.na(fnb_bw)) {
  # estimate & clamp bandwidth
  h_est <- tryCatch(spatstat.explore::bw.diggle(fnb_ppp), error = function(e) 400)
  h_est <- as.numeric(h_est)
  fnb_bw <- min(max(h_est, 300), 800)   # clamp 300–800 m

  kde_im <- spatstat.explore::density.ppp(
    fnb_ppp, sigma = fnb_bw, edge = TRUE, kernel = "gaussian"
  )

  saveRDS(kde_im, fnb_kde_rds)
  saveRDS(fnb_bw, fnb_bw_rds)
}

# --- Scale to per km^2 and convert to SpatRaster with CRS ---
kde_im_km2 <- kde_im * 1e6
kde_r <- terra::rast(kde_im_km2)
terra::crs(kde_r) <- "EPSG:3414"
if (!file.exists(fnb_kde_tif)) terra::writeRaster(kde_r, fnb_kde_tif, overwrite = TRUE)

# --- (Optional) map directly ---
tmap_mode("plot")
tm_shape(kde_r) +
  tm_raster(
    col.scale  = tm_scale_continuous(values = "Blues"),
    col.legend = tm_legend(title = "F&B intensity\n(registrations per km²)")
  ) +
  tm_shape(subzones_use) + tm_borders(col = "white", lwd = 0.3) +
  tm_shape(sf::st_as_sf(sf::st_make_valid(sf::st_union(subzones_use)))) +
  tm_borders(col = "black", lwd = 1.1) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)








Improving KDE Raster Interpretability
To improve the interpretability of the KDE raster and ensure consistency across sectors, we perform the following steps:

Clamp and winsorize values


Negative density values (possible from smoothing) are reset to zero.

Extremely high values above the 99th percentile are capped.

This reduces the influence of outliers and makes the colour scale more readable.


Define consistent breaks


Using the classInt package, compute six quantile-based breakpoints.

These can be reused across sectors (e.g., IT services, Logistics) to keep maps directly comparable.


Generate a cleaned raster


Create a new raster (kde_rw) with the adjusted values.


Thematic mapping


Plot the KDE with fixed breaks and a blue sequential palette.

White borders show planning areas, and a thick black outline marks the overall study area.

Place the legend outside the map for clarity.


# Clamp negatives, winsorize top tail for readability
vals <- terra::values(kde_r, mat = FALSE)
vals <- pmax(vals, 0)
cap <- as.numeric(quantile(vals, 0.99, na.rm = TRUE))   # 99th percentile cap
vals <- pmin(vals, cap)
kde_rw <- kde_r
terra::values(kde_rw) <- vals

# Pretty breaks (same set you can reuse for IT/Logistics for comparability)
library(classInt)
brks <- classInt::classIntervals(vals, n = 6, style = "quantile")$brks

tmap_mode("plot")
tm_shape(kde_rw) +
  tm_raster(
    style = "fixed", breaks = brks,
    col.scale = tm_scale_continuous(values = "Blues"),
    col.legend = tm_legend(title = "F&B intensity\n(registrations per km²)")
  ) +
  tm_shape(subzones_use) + tm_borders(col = "white", lwd = 0.25) +
  tm_shape(sf::st_as_sf(sf::st_make_valid(sf::st_union(subzones_use)))) +
  tm_borders(col = "black", lwd = 1.0) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE, component.autoscale = FALSE, legend.outside = TRUE)








F&B business registrations, KDE (Jan 2024–Jun 2025). Intensities shown as registrations per km².Bandwidth = 300 m.. The surface is zero-clamped and capped at the 99th percentile to enhance mid-range readability. Hot spots cluster around CBD/fringe-CBD and town-centre nodes; diffuse background reflects island-wide service presence.

6.2.1 Descriptive Statistics for the F&B KDE Surface
This section generates descriptive statistics for the F&B KDE surface:

Bandwidth retrieval:
The smoothing bandwidth used in KDE (fnb_bw) is loaded from cache if available, otherwise recomputed with bw.diggle and clamped between 300–800 m for stability.
Raster values:
Raw cell values from the KDE raster (kde_r, in registrations per km²) are extracted. Missing values are removed and any small negatives are clamped to zero.
Summary statistics:
From these values, we calculate:

total number of F&B points (n),

bandwidth (m),

mean and median intensity,

maximum intensity.

6.2.2 F&B (SSIC 56) – KDE Summary (Jan 2024–Jun 2025)
The kernel density estimation (KDE) of F&B registrations (n = 5,755) reveals strong clustering around the CBD, fringe-CBD, and major town-centre nodes. 6.3 Spatial Intensity of IT Services (SSIC 62) Business Registrations
This helper chunk sets up shared resources and utility functions for kernel density estimation (KDE):
Directory setup: Defines data/rds and data/rasters as cache locations, creating them if they don’t exist. These folders store RDS objects (intermediate results) and raster files (GeoTIFFs).
Analysis window: Ensures the spatial observation window W exists, created from the union of planning area polygons (subzones_use). This window defines the study area for point pattern analysis.
Breakpoints for comparability: Loads a set of fixed class breaks (kde_breaks_6.rds) that were saved from the F&B analysis. These breaks will be reused across sectors so that KDE maps are directly comparable.
Utility functions:
make_ppp(sf_pts, W): converts an sf point object into a ppp (planar point pattern) object within the window W.
compute_kde_cached(ppp_obj, rds_im, rds_bw): computes a Gaussian KDE for the given point pattern. If cached raster (im) and bandwidth (bw) exist, they are loaded; otherwise, a new bandwidth is estimated (bw.diggle, clamped between 300–800 m), KDE computed, and results saved.
to_raster_km2(im): converts a spatstat image into a SpatRaster, scaling values from per m² to per km² and assigning the correct CRS (EPSG:3414).

rds_dir     <- "data/rds"
rasters_dir <- "data/rasters"
dir.create(rds_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(rasters_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

# Ensure analysis window exists
if (!exists("W")) W <- spatstat.geom::as.owin(sf::st_union(subzones_use))

# Load the fixed breaks saved from the F&B map
brks_path <- file.path(rds_dir, "kde_breaks_6.rds")
stopifnot(file.exists(brks_path))  # ensure F&B saved these earlier
brks <- readRDS(brks_path)

# Small utilities
make_ppp <- function(sf_pts, W){
  xy <- sf::st_coordinates(sf_pts)
  spatstat.geom::ppp(xy[,1], xy[,2], window = W, check = FALSE)
}

compute_kde_cached <- function(ppp_obj, rds_im, rds_bw, sigma_min = 300, sigma_max = 800){
  if (file.exists(rds_im) && file.exists(rds_bw)) {
    list(im = readRDS(rds_im), bw = readRDS(rds_bw))
  } else {
    h_est <- tryCatch(spatstat.explore::bw.diggle(ppp_obj), error = function(e) 400)
    bw    <- min(max(as.numeric(h_est), sigma_min), sigma_max)
    im    <- spatstat.explore::density.ppp(ppp_obj, sigma = bw, edge = TRUE, kernel = "gaussian")
    saveRDS(im, rds_im); saveRDS(bw, rds_bw)
    list(im = im, bw = bw)
  }
}

to_raster_km2 <- function(im){
  r <- terra::rast(im * 1e6)   # per m^2 -> per km^2
  terra::crs(r) <- "EPSG:3414"
  r
}

This block reproduces the KDE workflow for the IT (SSIC 62) sector and plots it on the same scale as F&B for apples-to-apples comparison.

File paths:
Sets RDS/GeoTIFF cache targets for the IT KDE image (it_kde_im.rds), bandwidth (it_bw.rds), and raster (it_kde_per_km2.tif).
Point pattern setup:
Filters IT registrations from biz_pts_use, converts them to a ppp object within the study window W via make_ppp().
KDE with caching:

compute_kde_cached() loads precomputed KDE + bandwidth if present; otherwise it estimates bandwidth (Diggle, clamped 300–800 m), computes a Gaussian KDE, and caches both.

to_raster_km2() converts the KDE image to a SpatRaster and rescales units to registrations per km².

The raster is written once as a GeoTIFF for reuse.

Value cleaning (no winsorizing):
Negative cells are clamped to zero to remove smoothing artefacts. Unlike F&B, no top-tail winsorizing is applied here, because we will reuse the fixed breaks saved from F&B (brks) for strict comparability.
Mapping with shared breaks:
Plots the cleaned IT raster using style = "fixed" + breaks = brks (the exact class limits from F&B), a blue sequential scale, white subzone borders, and a black outer boundary.
The legend sits outside for clarity.

it_bw_rds <- file.path(rds_dir, "it_bw.rds")

# Build ppp

it_ppp <- make_ppp(it_sf, W)

6.5 Spatio Temporal KDE

6.5.1 Helpers (bandwidths, weights, KDE + caching)
This block sets up monthly spatio-temporal KDE helpers that produce per-sector rasters with spatial smoothing (meters) and temporal Gaussian weights (days), with caching. Bandwidth & Weights - get_sigma_m(ppp_obj, clamp=c(300,800)): estimates spatial KDE bandwidth via bw.diggle; coerces to numeric, defaults to 400 if failed, then clamps to 300–800 m for stability.
- time_weights(dates, t_center, tau_days=60): computes Gaussian temporal weights around a month center; normalizes weights to mean 1 so KDE magnitudes are comparable across months.
Building Inputs - ppp_for_sector(sector_name): filters biz_pts_use by sector, converts to ppp within w, and attaches reg_date as an attribute (used to derive temporal weights).
Monthly ST-KDE with Caching - stkde_month_slice(sector_name, t_center, sigma_m, tau_days=60, overwrite_tif=FALSE):
- Creates a month tag (YYYY-MM), derives cache file paths (stkde_<sector>_<YYYY-MM>.rds/.tif).
- Loads cached GeoTIFF/RDS if present (unless overwrite_tif=TRUE).
- Otherwise:
- Builds X (ppp) and pulls attached reg_date.
- Computes temporal weights for that month (tau_days = temporal bandwidth).
- Runs weighted spatial KDE:
r       density.ppp(X, sigma=sigma_m, edge=TRUE, kernel="gaussian", weights=w) - Saves the im (spatstat image) as RDS.
- Converts to per km² SpatRaster (* 1e6), clamps negatives to 0, sets CRS EPSG:3414, writes GeoTIFF, and returns the raster.

# Ensure folders
rds_dir     <- "data/rds"
rasters_dir <- "data/rasters"
dir.create(rds_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(rasters_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

# Ensure window W
if (!exists("W")) W <- spatstat.geom::as.owin(sf::st_union(subzones_use))

# Sectors you already defined
targets <- tibble::tibble(
  ssic2 = c("56", "62", "52"),
  sector = c("F&B (56)", "IT (62)", "Logistics/Warehousing (52)")
)

# -------- Spatial bandwidth (per sector) with clamps --------
get_sigma_m <- function(ppp_obj, clamp = c(300, 800)){
  h <- tryCatch(spatstat.explore::bw.diggle(ppp_obj), error = function(e) NA_real_)
  h <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(h))
  if (!is.finite(h)) h <- 400
  pmax(clamp[1], pmin(h, clamp[2]))
}

# -------- Temporal Gaussian weights (days) --------
# tau_days = temporal bandwidth (std dev) in days, e.g. 45–60
time_weights <- function(dates, t_center, tau_days = 60){
  dt <- as.numeric(dates - t_center)
  w  <- exp(-0.5 * (dt / tau_days)^2)
  # Normalize to mean 1 (keeps magnitudes comparable across months)
  if (mean(w) > 0) w <- w / mean(w)
  w
}

# -------- Build sector ppp with attributes --------
ppp_for_sector <- function(sector_name){
  pts <- dplyr::filter(biz_pts_use, sector == sector_name)
  xy  <- sf::st_coordinates(pts)
  X   <- spatstat.geom::ppp(xy[,1], xy[,2], window = W, check = FALSE)
  # Attach attributes for time weights
  attr(X, "reg_date") <- pts$reg_date
  X
}

# -------- Spatial KDE with temporal smoothing (weighted) + caching --------
# Returns a SpatRaster in registrations per km^2
stkde_month_slice <- function(sector_name, t_center, sigma_m, tau_days = 60,
                              overwrite_tif = FALSE){
  mon_tag <- format(t_center, "%Y-%m")  # YYYY-MM
  base    <- paste0(gsub("\\W","_", sector_name), "_", mon_tag)
  r_rds   <- file.path(rds_dir,     paste0("stkde_", base, ".rds"))
  r_tif   <- file.path(rasters_dir, paste0("stkde_", base, ".tif"))

  # If cached raster exists, load & return
  if (file.exists(r_tif) && !overwrite_tif) {
    r <- terra::rast(r_tif); return(r)
  }
  if (file.exists(r_rds) && !overwrite_tif) {
    im <- readRDS(r_rds)
  } else {
    X <- ppp_for_sector(sector_name)
    dates <- attr(X, "reg_date")
    stopifnot(inherits(dates, "Date"))

    # Temporal weights for this month
    w <- time_weights(dates, t_center = t_center, tau_days = tau_days)

    # Spatial KDE with Gaussian kernel + edge correction + weights
    im <- spatstat.explore::density.ppp(
      X, sigma = sigma_m, edge = TRUE, kernel = "gaussian", weights = w
    )
    saveRDS(im, r_rds)
  }

  # Convert to per km^2 raster, clamp small negatives to 0
  r <- terra::rast(im * 1e6); terra::crs(r) <- "EPSG:3414"
  vals <- terra::values(r, mat = FALSE)
  vals <- pmax(vals, 0)
  terra::values(r) <- vals

  terra::writeRaster(r, r_tif, overwrite = TRUE)
  r
}



6.5.2 Define the month grid and sector bandwidths
The code chunk below helps us define the following Month centers
- months_vec: mid-month dates from 15 Jan 2024 → 15 Jun 2025 (interval = 1 month).
- Used as temporal centers for Gaussian time weights.
Sector point patterns & bandwidths
- sector_ppp: list to store sector-wise ppp objects (F&B, IT, Logistics).
- sector_bw: numeric vector to store each sector’s optimal spatial bandwidth.
Loop over sectors (targets$sector)
1. ppp_for_sector(sec) → builds point pattern with registration dates.
2. Store in sector_ppp.
3. get_sigma_m(X, clamp=c(300,800)) → computes Diggle bandwidth (300–800 m), stored in sector_bw.
Output
- sector_bw = chosen bandwidths per sector, reused across all monthly KDE runs.

# Build ppp for each sector once, get spatial bandwidths

sector_bw  <- setNames(numeric(length(targets$sector)), targets$sector)

for (sec in targets$sector) {
  X <- ppp_for_sector(sec)
  sector_ppp[[sec]] <- X
  sector_bw[[sec]]  <- get_sigma_m(X, clamp = c(300, 800))
}

6.5.3 Run ST-KDE (monthly slices) for all sectors
This block runs the monthly spatio-temporal KDE for each sector. It loops over all sectors and months, applying stkde_month_slice() with sector-specific bandwidths and a temporal smoothing window (tau_days = 60), returning cached SpatRaster intensity maps for each sector–month combination.

# Choose temporal bandwidth (days). 60 ~ two months std dev → smooths but keeps seasonality.
tau_days <- 60

# Compute & cache every sector × month; returns list of lists of SpatRasters
stkde_all <- lapply(targets$sector, function(sec){
  sigma_m <- sector_bw[[sec]]
  lapply(months_vec, function(t0){
    stkde_month_slice(sec, t_center = t0, sigma_m = sigma_m, tau_days = tau_days)
  })
})

6.5.4 Shared breaks for comparability (derive once, reuse)
This block samples raster values from a chosen period (e.g., 2025-H1 across all sectors) to derive quantile-based class breaks. It pools values, clamps negatives to zero, computes 6 quantile breaks, and saves them for consistent color scaling across all monthly maps.

for (sec in targets$sector) {
  for (i in sel_idx) {
    v <- terra::values(stkde_all[[sec]][[i]], mat = FALSE)
    vals_sample <- c(vals_sample, v[is.finite(v)])
  }
}
vals_sample <- pmax(vals_sample, 0)
brks6 <- classInt::classIntervals(vals_sample, n = 6, style = "quantile")$brks
saveRDS(brks6, file.path(rds_dir, "stkde_month_breaks6.rds"))



6.5.5 Faceted map for a chosen semester (e.g., 2025-Jan → 2025-Jun)
Helper function to create faceted monthly maps of spatio-temporal KDE intensity for a chosen semester (default: Jan–Jun 2025).
Process
- Inputs: sector name, start and end dates.
- Subset months: select indices of months_vec within the semester, extract KDE rasters from stkde_all.
- Singapore outline: build boundary polygon for clean framing.
- Map creation (per month)
- Plot raster with fixed breaks (brks6) → ensures comparability across months.
- Add subzone borders (thin white) + outer boundary (black).
- Title with sector + month; legend only on first map.
- Faceting: combine monthly maps side-by-side using tmap_arrange() (3 columns).

brks6 <- readRDS(file.path(rds_dir, "stkde_month_breaks6.rds"))

plot_semester <- function(sec, start = as.Date("2025-01-01"), end = as.Date("2025-06-30")){
  idx <- which(months_vec >= start & months_vec <= end)
  rlist <- stkde_all[[sec]][idx]
  # Build a small sf outline for nice border
  sg_outline <- subzones_use |> sf::st_union() |> sf::st_make_valid() |> sf::st_as_sf()

  # tmap: one facet per month
  tmaps <- lapply(seq_along(rlist), function(i){
    mon_lab <- format(months_vec[idx][i], "%b %Y")
    tm_shape(rlist[[i]]) +
      tm_raster(
        style = "fixed", breaks = brks6,
        col.scale  = tm_scale_continuous(values = "Blues"),
        col.legend = tm_legend(title = "Intensity\n(registrations per km²)")
      ) +
      tm_shape(subzones_use) + tm_borders(col = "white", lwd = 0.25) +
      tm_shape(sg_outline)   + tm_borders(col = "black", lwd = 1.0) +
      tm_layout(title = paste0(sec, " — ", mon_lab),
                legend.show = i == 1,  # show once
                frame = FALSE)
  })
  tmap::tmap_arrange(plotlist = tmaps, ncol = 3)
}

7 2nd Order Spatio Temporal Analysis
While first-order analysis revealed density surfaces of business activity, it did not answer whether these businesses simply follow background intensity (CBD, industrial corridors, malls) or whether they also exhibit interaction effects — clustering in both space and time beyond random expectation. To address this, we employ second-order spatio-temporal analysis (Ripley’s K/L, pair correlation, Knox test, and space–time K-function). These methods allow us to quantify the scales at which new firms tend to emerge together, and whether such patterns differ across sectors (F&B, IT, Logistics). By identifying these interaction ranges, we can link firm behaviour to urban form, infrastructure readiness, and zoning policy — providing actionable spatial intelligence for planners.

7.1 Singapore-wide second-order space–time tests
Parameters and Functions for Spatio-Temporal (ST) Point Pattern Analysis
This helper block sets up the parameters and functions needed for spatio-temporal (ST) point pattern analysis.

Time window:
Defines the period of study: from 1 Jan 2024 (t0) to 30 Jun 2025 (t1).
All business registrations outside this range will be excluded from the analysis.
Study boundary:
Unions all planning subzones into one boundary polygon (sg_union), then converts it into a simple (x,y) coordinate matrix bdry.
This format is required by splancs::stkhat() for ST K-function computation.
Point conversion function (as_xyz):
Converts an sf point layer into a numeric matrix with three columns:

x, y: planar coordinates (SVY21 metres),

t: registration time, expressed as days since t0.

It ensures only points with registration dates inside the study window are included, and matches them by unique ID (uen) to keep attributes and geometry aligned.
Grid definitions:

r_vals: spatial distance lags (metres) for the ST K-function, finer at short ranges (50 m steps up to 500 m) and coarser at larger ranges (up to 4 km).

u_vals: temporal lags (days) ranging from 1 week to ~6 months.

Simulation settings:

nsim = 199: number of Monte Carlo simulations (199 for drafting, increase to 999 for final results).

set.seed(626): ensures reproducibility of simulations.

Normalizing stkhat() Output with fix_dims()
We define fix_dims() to reshape results from splancs::stkhat() into a consistent ns × nu matrix:

If a list → unlist() and reshape to ns × nu.

If a vector →

length == ns*nu: reshape directly.

length == ns or nu: stop with clear error.

Else: try as.matrix(K) and adjust:

If already ns × nu, use.

If nu × ns, transpose.

Otherwise, throw informative error.



Force double precision (storage.mode(M) <- "double") for compatibility.


fix_dims <- function(K, ns, nu){
  # splancs::stkhat() can return:
  # - a matrix (ns x nu), or
  # - a list (often length ns, each element length nu), or
  # - a vector (ns*nu)
  if (is.list(K)) {
    v <- unlist(K, use.names = FALSE)     # flatten list to numeric
    M <- matrix(v, nrow = ns, ncol = nu, byrow = TRUE)
  } else {
    v <- as.numeric(K)
    if (length(v) == ns * nu) {
      M <- matrix(v, nrow = ns, ncol = nu)
    } else if (length(v) == ns || length(v) == nu) {
      stop("stkhat() returned a length-", length(v),
           " vector; expected ns*nu = ", ns*nu, ".")
    } else {
      # try to coerce if it's a 2D object with swapped dims
      M0 <- try(as.matrix(K), silent = TRUE)
      if (inherits(M0, "try-error")) {
        stop("stkhat() returned unexpected type/shape.")
      }
      if (all(dim(M0) == c(ns, nu))) {
        M <- M0
      } else if (all(dim(M0) == c(nu, ns))) {
        M <- t(M0)
      } else {
        stop("stkhat() returned matrix with dims ",
             paste(dim(M0), collapse="x"),
             " but expected ", ns, "x", nu, ".")
      }
    }
  }
  storage.mode(M) <- "double"
  M
}
